strings.BRB_Acing_the_Report_Card_desc:
Following a wave of riots across the Caribbean in 1952, the joint Canadian-American advisory committee known as the West Indies Commission created an ambitious development plan to remake the region. Ten years later, the results have been uneven to say the least, lack of funding and reactionary administrators have stymied these grand plans. And yet, despite the odds, the fledgling state of Barbados stands above the rest, providing a modern level of education, healthcare, and economic mobility for its population.

At the same time, with an increasingly investor-friendly economy, American capital has begun flowing into Bridgetown in droves to aid in the nation's development, and overbearing foreign advisors and businessmen dictate policy from above. Some Bajans are beginning to wonder if development is truly worth the price of a new colonialism.
strings.BRB_Growing_National_Consciouness_desc:
As the Caribbean joins in a united struggle to leave behind antiquated colonialism, a growing demand for autonomy has become apparent in Barbados in the advent of a gestating Bajan patriotic tradition. With locals from all castes realizing the indifference of the Ottawan bosses regarding the needs of their southern subjects, the Bajan public has come under the rallying call of pan-Caribbeanism, propagating throughout the region. Conscious of the nation's strategic strengths, Bridgetown's activists particularly emphasize the leading role of Barbados as a role model of economic and political freedom.

By and large, most Bajans have become somewhat receptive to the idea of further integration into the broader independent Caribbean community, and for the courageous, dreaming of the island-states united is not far beyond their wildest imagination.
strings.BRB_Party_Monopoly_desc:
A one-way crossroad is the best way to describe the party politics of Barbados; oftentimes, there's less of an illusion of choice than an artificial pretense of such. Having been the sole power-broker in Barbados' playground since the 1930s, the Barbados Labour Party had made its full command over essentially the entire nation an open secret under the jurisdiction of Grantley Adams and his protégés.

Despite employing a relatively progressive approach to social concerns, Adams' Anglophile tendencies never managed to win over much of the younger, more independent-minded Bajans — having become increasingly unsupported by the public throughout the past years. It will nevertheless be very difficult, however, to remove the BLP from a position of power, on account of the favors and leverage it'd gathered throughout the years.
